b2016-1.ask: Which traffic sign has the most lines of symmetry?
steps: A line of symmetry is a fold line where both halves land exactly on each other.
Try folding each sign across the middle (left to right) and down the middle (top to bottom).
A folds evenly only across the middle: 1 line. E folds evenly only down the middle: 1 line. B and D don't fold evenly at all.
C folds evenly BOTH ways: 2 lines. That's the most.
b2016-1.check: Fold C across the middle: the halves match. Fold it down the middle: they match again. ✓
b2016-1.spot: Symmetry? Imagine folding along a line and check if the halves land on each other.
b2016-1.oops: Thinking a circle has lots of lines, without noticing the picture inside spoils most of them.

b2016-2.ask: Pizza cut into quarters, then each quarter into thirds. What part of the pizza is one piece?
steps: 4 quarters, each cut into 3 pieces.
4 × 3 = 12 equal pieces.
One piece is 1/12 of the pizza.
b2016-2.spot: Cutting pieces into smaller pieces? Multiply to count all the pieces.

b2016-3.ask: A 10 cm thread is folded into equal zigzag parts and cut at two marked places. How long are the three pieces?
steps: Count the equal parts the folded thread makes: 10. So each part is 1 cm.
The cuts split the thread into three pieces. Count how many 1 cm parts are in each piece.
The pieces have 2, 3 and 5 parts.
So they're 2 cm, 3 cm and 5 cm.
b2016-3.spot: Folded things? Count the equal parts first to find one part's length.
b2016-3.oops: Guessing from how long the pieces look in the picture.

b2016-4.ask: 8 magnets hold up postcards. What's the most magnets Lisa can remove without any postcard falling?
steps: Each postcard needs at least one magnet. Find the fewest magnets you must keep; the rest can go.
The cards form two groups. In the top group, one magnet holds both overlapping cards, so keep just 1 magnet there.
In the bottom group, one magnet holds three overlapping cards. Two more cards don't overlap each other, so each needs its own magnet: 3 magnets there.
Keep 1 + 3 = 4 magnets. So 8 − 4 = 4 can be removed.
b2016-4.check: Point at the 4 magnets you keep: every card is under at least one of them. ✓
b2016-4.spot: Most you can remove? Find the fewest you must keep.
b2016-4.oops: Forgetting that one magnet can hold two cards where they overlap.

b2016-5.ask: Join the midpoints of a 10 cm square's sides. What's the area of the smaller square?
steps: Draw lines across the middle of the big square, making 4 small squares (5 × 5 each).
The green square cuts each small square exactly in half along its diagonal.
So the green square is half of the big square.
Big square: 10 × 10 = 100. Half: 50 cm².
b2016-5.check: The 4 white corner triangles also add up to 50. 50 + 50 = 100. ✓
b2016-5.spot: Tilted shapes inside squares? Cut the square into pieces you understand.
b2016-5.oops: Guessing 25 because the side looks half as long.

b2016-6.ask: Each plate needs a knife on the right and a fork on the left. Fewest knife-fork swaps?
steps: Look at each plate: which ones are wrong?
Some plates have the fork and knife on the wrong sides, and some have two of the same thing.
A swap can fix two problems at once if you swap a misplaced knife with a misplaced fork.
Two swaps fix everything.
b2016-6.check: After the 2 swaps, every plate has fork left, knife right. ✓
b2016-6.spot: Fewest swaps? Make each swap fix two wrong things at once.
b2016-6.oops: Counting how many things are wrong instead of how many swaps fix them.

b2016-7.ask: A centipede has 100 feet and 25 pairs of shoes. How many more shoes does it need?
steps: 25 pairs = 25 × 2 = 50 shoes.
It needs 100 shoes, one per foot.
100 − 50 = 50 more shoes.
b2016-7.spot: Pairs? Change pairs into single items first.

b2016-8.ask: Tom and John build boxes with the same number of cubes. How many levels will John's box have?
steps: Count Tom's cubes: his box is 6 long, 2 wide and 2 high. 6 × 2 × 2 = 24 cubes.
John's first level is 3 × 2 = 6 cubes.
24 cubes ÷ 6 per level = 4 levels.
b2016-8.check: John's box: 4 levels of 6 = 24 cubes, same as Tom's. ✓
b2016-8.spot: Same total, different shape? Count the total, then divide by one layer.
b2016-8.oops: Only counting the cubes you can see in Tom's picture.

b2016-9.ask: Four girls in four beds. Bea and Pia face each other; Mary and Karen have their backs to each other. How many lie on their right side?
steps: Try it yourself: lie down facing someone. If your friend lies the same way (head on the same side), one of you is on your right side and the other on your left.
Bea and Pia face each other with heads on the same side: one is on her right side, one on her left.
Mary and Karen face away from each other, heads on the same side: again, one right, one left.
So 1 + 1 = 2 girls are on their right side.
b2016-9.check: Act it out with a friend or two toys. ✓
b2016-9.spot: Left, right and facing? Act it out with your body.
b2016-9.oops: Thinking 'facing each other' means both on the same side.

b2016-10.ask: A paper net is folded into an open box. Which face is the bottom?
steps: The bottom of an open box touches all four side walls.
Look at the net: A B on top, C D E below, with B above C.
Fold it in your head with B flat: A folds up on one side, C folds up below, and D and E wrap around to make the other walls.
B is the face that touches every other face. It's the bottom.
b2016-10.check: Fold a paper copy and see: A, C, D, E stand up around B. ✓
b2016-10.spot: Nets of boxes? Find the face that touches all the walls.
b2016-10.oops: Choosing the face in the middle of the long row (D) without folding.

b2016-11.ask: Which shape can't be made by gluing these two equal squares together?
steps: Each shape must be made of exactly two squares of the same size, overlapping or touching.
Check each picture: can you see two equal squares inside it?
B is two squares turned like a star. C is two squares side by side. D is two squares overlapping corner to corner. E is a square and a turned square.
A has a triangle on top that doesn't fit inside a square of the same size. It can't be made.
b2016-11.check: Trace two squares onto A: the pointed top always sticks out. ✓
b2016-11.spot: Which can't be made? Try to build each one from the pieces you're given.
b2016-11.oops: Picking B because it looks complicated.

b2016-12.ask: Monday to Friday, exactly two of Mary, Ann and Nata work each day. Mary works 3 days, Ann 4. How many days does Nata work?
steps: 5 days × 2 people = 10 work-days in total.
Mary 3 + Ann 4 = 7.
Nata: 10 − 7 = 3 days.
b2016-12.spot: Shifts or turns? Count the total spots, then take away what's known.
b2016-12.oops: Thinking only one person works each day.

b2016-13.ask: Five squirrels run to the nearest nut at the same speed, then to the next nearest. Which squirrel gets two nuts?
steps: Look at the number line: count the marks between each squirrel and the nuts.
Move ALL the squirrels at once, one step at a time. Each runs to its closest nut.
Step 1: A, C, D and E each grab a nut. Step 3: B grabs one. Now every squirrel has one nut and one nut is left.
C is closest to that last nut, so C gets two nuts.
b2016-13.check: Write down which nut each squirrel grabs and when: 6 nuts, 5 squirrels, and C gets two. ✓
b2016-13.spot: Things moving at the same time? Go one step at a time for everyone.
b2016-13.oops: Moving one squirrel all the way before the others.

b2016-15.ask: Cut the strip 2581953764 twice to make 3 numbers. What's the smallest sum?
steps: 10 digits into 3 numbers. To keep the sum small, no number should be too long: 4 + 3 + 3 digits.
The 4-digit number matters most. Make it start with the smallest digit: 1.
There's a 1 in the middle: 258 | 1953 | 764.
b2016-15.check: Other cuts give bigger 4-digit numbers, like 2581 + 953 + 764 = 4298. ✓
b2016-15.spot: Making a small sum? Keep the longest number as small as possible.
b2016-15.oops: Cutting into equal-looking pieces without checking which number is longest.

b2016-16.ask: Bart sees a clock in a mirror. What would the mirror show 10 minutes earlier?
steps: A mirror swaps left and right. The mirror clock looks like 1:45, so the real clock shows 10:15.
Go back 10 minutes on the real clock: 10:05.
Now mirror 10:05: it looks like 1:55.
Find the picture that looks like 1:55: E.
b2016-16.check: Mirror 1:55 back: 10:05, which is 10 minutes before 10:15. ✓
b2016-16.spot: Mirror clocks? Turn it into a real time, do the math, then mirror back.
b2016-16.oops: Moving the hands backwards in the mirror picture (that's forwards in real life).

b2016-18.ask: BENJAMIN uses digits 1 to 7, same letters same digits. It's odd and divides by 3. What digit is N?
steps: BENJAMIN has 8 letters but only 7 different ones: B, E, N, J, A, M, I. N appears twice.
So the digits 1 to 7 are each used once, plus N one more time. Digit sum = 28 + N.
To divide by 3, 28 + N must divide by 3: N = 2 or 5.
The number is odd, and it ends in N. So N is odd: 5.
b2016-18.check: 28 + 5 = 33, which divides by 3 ✓, and it ends in 5, odd ✓.
b2016-18.spot: Divides by 3? Add up the digits. Odd? Look at the last digit.

b2016-19.ask: Triplets and their brother who is 3 years younger. Which could be the total of all four ages?
steps: If the triplets are each T, the brother is T − 3.
Total = T + T + T + T − 3 = 4 × T − 3.
So total + 3 must divide by 4.
b2016-19.spot: People with ages related to each other? Write everyone in terms of one age.
b2016-19.oops: Forgetting the brother is younger, not older.

b2016-21.ask: A circle of paper is folded three times, cut along a line, and unfolded. What does the middle part look like?
steps: Unfold one step at a time, starting with the LAST fold.
The cut is one straight line. Each unfold mirrors it across the fold line, so it doubles: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 lines.
Draw the 8 cut lines around the centre: together they make the outline of the middle piece.
That outline matches picture D.
b2016-21.check: Fold a paper circle three times and snip it the same way. ✓
b2016-21.spot: Folding and cutting? Unfold one fold at a time and mirror the cut each time.
b2016-21.oops: Picking the shape with the most notches without checking.

b2016-22.ask: Numbers that start with 1, each next digit at least as big as the one before, digits adding to 5. How many?
steps: Make an ordered list, shortest numbers first.
4 digits: 1112. 5 digits: 11111. That's all.
b2016-22.check: Each digit is at least the one before, each starts with 1, each adds to 5. ✓
b2016-22.spot: Counting numbers with rules? List them by length, in order.

b2016-23.ask: How many L-shapes made of 4 squares can be cut from a 5 × 5 square?
steps: The square has 25 small squares. Each L uses 4.
7 L-shapes would need 28 squares. Too many. So at most 6.
Try to fit 6: with careful arrangement, 6 L-shapes fit (using 24 squares, 1 left over).
So the answer is 6.
b2016-23.check: Draw a 5 × 5 grid and fit 6 L-shapes. ✓
b2016-23.spot: How many fit? Area gives a limit; then try to reach it.
b2016-23.oops: Saying 5 because it's hard to fit 6 at first try.

b2016-24.ask: With all tables single (4 chairs each), Luigi needs 6 more chairs. With double tables (6 chairs each), he has 4 left over. How many tables?
steps: Single tables: 4 chairs per table. Double tables: 2 tables share 6 chairs, which is 3 per table.
So switching from single to double saves 1 chair per table.
From '6 chairs short' to '4 chairs extra' is a change of 10 chairs.
1 chair per table saves 10 chairs: 10 tables.
b2016-24.check: 10 tables: singles need 40 chairs, he has 34 (6 short ✓). Doubles need 30, 4 left ✓.
b2016-24.spot: Two ways of sharing that give different leftovers? Find how much each item changes.
b2016-24.oops: Using 6 chairs per table for doubles. That's per pair of tables.

b2016-27.ask: A pentagon has 10 circles, 5 already filled. Fill the rest so every side's three numbers add the same. What is X?
steps: Two sides that share a corner circle have the same sum, so the OTHER two circles on each side must add to the same amount.
The side with 3 and the side with 1 share a corner: 7 + 3 = 1 + y, so the bottom-left circle y = 9.
Now the bottom side and the lower-right side share a corner: 9 + 6 = 2 + X.
b2016-27.check: Fill in all circles and add each side: every side gives the same sum. ✓
b2016-27.spot: Equal sums around a shape? Compare neighbouring sides and cancel what they share.
b2016-27.oops: Guessing numbers without using the sides that share circles.

b2016-28.ask: ○□○ has digit sum □△. □△ has digit sum □. What digit is ○?
steps: □△ has digit sum □. So □ + △ = □, which means △ = 0.
So □△ = □0, a two-digit number ending in 0 (10 times □).
Digits only: □ = 2 and ○ = 9.
b2016-28.spot: Symbol puzzles? Find the easiest clue first. Here △ must be 0.
b2016-28.oops: Starting with the 3-digit number, the hardest part.

b2016-29.ask: Start at 12. Multiply or divide by 2 or 3, exactly 60 times. Which result is impossible?
steps: 12 = 2 × 2 × 3. Each step adds or removes one 2 or one 3.
60 steps is an even number. Steps that cancel (×2 then ÷2) come in pairs.
So the number of 2s and 3s you change, added together, must be EVEN.
36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3: just one extra 3 (odd). Impossible. The others need an even number of changes.
b2016-29.spot: Lots of steps? Look at odd and even: how many steps does each answer need?
b2016-29.oops: Thinking 36 is easy because 12 × 3 = 36. That's 1 step, and 59 more must cancel out, which can't happen.

b2016-30.ask: Two 3-digit numbers use 6 different digits. The second's first digit is twice the first's last digit. What's the smallest sum?
steps: To keep the sum small, the hundreds digits should be small.
If the first number starts with 1, it can't end in 1, so it ends in 2 and the second starts with 4.
Use the smallest digits left for the tens and ones: 0, 3, 5. First 102, second 435.
102 + 435 = 537. (Starting the second number with 2 forces the first to start with 3 or more: 301 + 245 = 546, bigger.)
b2016-30.spot: Smallest sum? Make the hundreds digits as small as possible first.
b2016-30.oops: Starting the second number with 2 without checking it forces bigger hundreds.
